context: heavy civil · river diversion and dam by dry seasons; turbines embedded in the powerhouse concrete

brief.intro: New to this project type? A hydropower plant stores or diverts river water, drops it through turbines and returns it to the river. Most of the job is heavy civil work in a river valley: divert the river through tunnels or channels behind cofferdams, excavate to sound rock, build the dam and the spillway, drive tunnels and a penstock to the powerhouse, and build the powerhouse itself. The turbines and generators are made over two or more years and installed in a strict sequence in which steel parts are set and then concreted in, stage by stage. The river sets the calendar: diversion and closure can only be done in the dry season, and a missed season is a lost year. At the end, the reservoir is filled under control and each unit is tested wet and connected to the grid.

must_get_right: Build the schedule around the river: diversion, cofferdam closure and reservoir filling are tied to dry seasons and flood seasons. Show the seasons on the calendar and the float to each.
Access roads, quarry and concrete plants in a remote valley are a project before the project — they decide when the main works can really start.

Turbine embedded parts are needed long before the turbines: draft tube and spiral case arrive first and are concreted in stages, so manufacture, delivery and powerhouse concrete must be planned as one sequence.
Geology is the main risk; hold contingency in excavation, tunnelling and foundation treatment rather than at the end.

basis_of_planning.standard: AACE Recommended Practice 38R-06 — Documenting the Schedule Basis

sections.heading: Scheduling method & tools
sections.body: A Critical Path Method (CPM) network built in Primavera P6, developed to a Level 3 control schedule with retained-logic progress. Activities are organised by structure (diversion, dam, spillway, waterways, powerhouse) and, inside the powerhouse, by generating unit.

sections.heading: Calendars & working time
sections.body: Site calendar with dry and flood seasons marked; river works and dam placement rates differ by season. Underground works run around the clock.

sections.heading: Sequencing logic & critical path
sections.body: Access → diversion → river closure in a dry season → foundation excavation and treatment → dam and spillway. Waterways and powerhouse in parallel. Powerhouse: first-stage concrete → crane → embedded parts → second-stage concrete → turbine → generator. Then dry tests → impoundment → wet tests → synchronisation, unit by unit. The critical path normally runs through diversion and the dam, or through the first unit.

sections.heading: Key assumptions
sections.body: River closure and impoundment happen in the planned seasons; geology is as investigated; land and resettlement are complete before impoundment; the transmission line is ready for back-energisation.

sections.heading: Procurement & long-lead items
sections.body: The schedule tracks the following as milestones because they drive the programme:

rows: Embedded parts first, then units to the erection sequence

sections.heading: Access, resource & site constraints
sections.body: Remote site with a single access; floods can overtop cofferdams; underground works limit the number of faces; heavy equipment needs road and bridge capacity checks.

sections.heading: Risks, float & contingency
sections.body: Main risks: floods, worse rock than expected, tunnel inflows, late embedded parts, resettlement delaying impoundment, and transmission-line readiness. Contingency is held before river closure and before impoundment.

sections.heading: Schedule levels of detail
sections.body: Reported at Level 1 (milestones) and Level 2 (summary) to the client; controlled at Level 3 by structure and generating unit; expanded to Level 4–5 lookahead for the excavation, concrete and erection crews — consistent with AACE 37R-06.
